overview: Lizard Point is as far south as you can go on the British mainland: a rugged headland of dark rock and wildflowers at the tip of the Lizard peninsula, with the sea on three sides. The National Trust looks after the land around it.

There’s something stirring about standing at the very end of Britain, and the coast here has a long and dramatic history. The waters around the Lizard were once nicknamed the ‘Graveyard of Ships’, which is why the Lizard Lighthouse was built on the point in 1752 and a lifeboat station still operates nearby.

expect.title: The point
expect.text: Clifftop paths lead out to the southernmost tip, with views along the coast in both directions and plenty of seabirds wheeling below.

expect.title: The lighthouse
expect.text: The Lizard Lighthouse, first built in 1752, stands on the headland and is a landmark for miles around.

expect.title: Coast path walks
expect.text: The South West Coast Path runs right past, so you can walk west to Kynance Cove or east to Housel Bay and Cadgwith.

goodToKnow.label: Where it is
goodToKnow.text: Just south of Lizard village, at the end of the A3083 from Helston.

goodToKnow.label: Before you go
goodToKnow.text: Check the National Trust website for current parking arrangements and facilities.

week.text: A must for most Lizard days: combine it with Kynance Cove at low tide and you’ve got one of the classic Cornish days out. It’s exposed, so it’s at its most atmospheric on a breezy day and pleasantest on a calm one.

pairWith.why: the famous serpentine cove, a short way west
a quiet sandy cove just to the east
a little fishing village further along the coast

tips: Bring a windproof: there’s nothing between you and the open sea.
Combine it with Kynance and time that part of the day for low tide.
